g.text: code is the clustered primary key, because GET /{code} is 99.9% of all queries
A surrogate id would make the one query the system exists to serve cost two B-tree descents instead of one.
Why code is the PK, not a surrogate id
On a clustered engine the row data lives in the leaf of
the code index - so GET /{code} is ONE descent and you
have the whole row. With a surrogate id it is two:
descend code -> find id -> descend the primary index.
At 5,800 reads/sec that is 5,800 avoidable descents a
second, forever, to gain a key nothing in the design uses.
Why long_url_hash is indexed but NOT unique
Unique here would enforce deduplication - the exact
product behaviour the design rejected, because it
collapses expiry, deletion, ownership and analytics
onto one row. It exists for abuse takedown instead.
Why a hash rather than indexing long_url
long_url averages 200 bytes with a long tail past 500 -
a wide, variable-length, poor index key. A fixed 8-byte
hash is dense and uniform. Truncated-hash collisions
do happen, so queries re-verify long_url in the WHERE.
One row per namespace. Sharding it would defeat its purpose - it
scales by namespace instead, giving each region a disjoint band.
Forensics for the one failure that matters: a coordinator failover
double-issuing a block, or a restored snapshot rewinding the counter.
Strong, read-your-writes. A stale miss here mints a second link.
Where the expensive guarantee is actually spent
urls strong on the WRITE, then freely eventual on reads - because the row is IMMUTABLE once written
code_counter strictly linearizable, and it is touched once per 100,000 links, so it costs almost nothing
Redis cache eventual, bounded by a TTL clamped to min(1 hour, time until expiry)
click events eventual, at-least-once - a double-counted click is a rounding error
The luckiest property in this design: the strong-consistency requirement applies to a
single-row insert whose shard key IS the code - so it needs no cross-shard
coordination, and the read path inherits none of it.
Both the read and the write derive the
shard from the only input either path
has - so every operation is single-shard.
